learningObjective: Design a golden test for a custom kernel by choosing an appropriate reference implementation, deterministic inputs, and tolerance schema.
stem: You are writing a golden test for a new fused Triton `LayerNorm(x) * gamma + beta` kernel. Which combination of design choices best matches golden-test discipline?
codeSnippet:
# Custom Triton kernel under test:
def fused_ln_gamma_beta(x, gamma, beta, eps=1e-5):
    ...

# Reference options:
#   (i)  torch.nn.functional.layer_norm on CUDA in FP32
#   (ii) A hand-written numpy CPU LayerNorm in FP64
#   (iii) An older version of the same Triton kernel

# Input options:
#   (a) torch.randn seeded with a fixed torch.manual_seed(0)
#   (b) Different random inputs every test invocation

# Tolerance options:
#   (α) rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-2 (BF16-appropriate)
#   (β) rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-6 (FP32/FP64-appropriate)
#   (γ) tolerance derived from the input dtype (FP32 rtol~1e-5, BF16 rtol~1e-2)

options.text: Reference (ii) — numpy CPU FP64; input (a) — fixed seed; tolerance (γ) — dtype-driven. A high-precision independent reference plus deterministic inputs plus dtype-appropriate tolerance is the strongest correctness signal, with the extra property that a floating-point-order difference between the CUDA implementation and the reference does not falsely fail the test.

Reference (iii) — an older version of the same kernel; input (b) — random each run; tolerance (β) — FP32 strict. Using the same-family reference guarantees the closest numerical match, and random inputs each run maximize coverage across the input distribution over CI history.

Reference (i) — torch.nn.functional.layer_norm; input (a) — fixed seed; tolerance (β) — strict FP32/FP64 tolerance regardless of the actual input dtype. Golden tests should always assert bitwise-close equality; letting BF16 tests pass at 1e-2 masks real bugs.

Reference — none; input (b) — random; tolerance (α) — loose BF16 tolerance. Golden tests are only useful for detecting NaN/Inf; numerical correctness is validated by end-to-end model accuracy on validation datasets, not by per-kernel numerical checks.

explanation: A robust golden test uses (i) an independent high-precision reference so the test does not merely re-check the buggy implementation against itself, (ii) deterministic inputs so failures are reproducible, and (iii) tolerances matched to the numeric dtype under test. Applying an FP64 tolerance to a BF16 kernel would guarantee failure; applying a BF16 tolerance to an FP32 test would hide bugs. Option B is anti-pattern (same-family reference); C sets a wrong tolerance floor; D abandons numerical validation entirely.

optionExplanations.B: Wrong: same-family reference invites shared bugs; random inputs make failure debugging painful.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: applying FP64 tolerance to BF16 kernels guarantees false failures.

assumptions: The CUDA implementation is being validated against a reference for correctness.
The test runs in CI where reproducibility matters.
nonImplications: Does not imply CPU/FP64 references are always feasible; some ops have no straightforward CPU reference.
Does not imply differential testing on random inputs is bad; it is complementary, not a replacement for a golden test.
